title: Ad Hominem
description: Attacking the person making an argument instead of addressing the argument itself.
content:
Visualize ARGUMENT │ ▼ ┌───────────┐ │ PERSON │ ← ATTACK └───────────┘ ✕ ARGUMENT IGNORED Definition An ad hominem argument attacks the person making an argument rather than addressing the argument itself.
Example “Don’t listen to Sarah’s argument about climate policy. She doesn’t even have a college degree.”
Why It’s Fallacious Sarah’s education has no bearing on whether her argument is correct. The argument should be evaluated based on its evidence and reasoning, not on characteristics of the person presenting it.
How to Recognize It Ask yourself:
“Is this response addressing the argument, or attacking the person making it?”
If the response attacks the person instead of addressing the substance of their argument, it may be an ad hominem fallacy.
Related Concepts Ad hominem arguments can take several forms, including attacks on someone’s character, circumstances, motives, or hypocrisy rather than the substance of their argument.

title: Ambiguity
description: Using an unclear or ambiguous statement to support a conclusion without resolving its possible meanings.
content:
Definition The ambiguity fallacy occurs when an argument depends on a statement that can reasonably be interpreted in multiple ways, without establishing which meaning is intended.
Example “The sign says the store is for everyone, so anyone can enter at any time.”
The phrase “for everyone” does not necessarily mean the store is open at all times.
Why It’s Fallacious An argument cannot rely on an interpretation that has not been established when other reasonable interpretations are possible.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“Could this statement reasonably mean more than one thing?”
If the argument depends on one particular interpretation, that interpretation needs to be established.

title: Amphiboly
description: Using a grammatically ambiguous statement in a way that exploits or ignores its possible interpretations.
content:
Definition Amphiboly occurs when the grammatical structure of a statement allows multiple interpretations and an argument relies on one interpretation without establishing it.
Example “I saw the man with the telescope.”
This could mean that I used a telescope to see the man, or that the man had the telescope.
Why It’s Fallacious The argument treats an ambiguous grammatical construction as though its intended meaning were unambiguous.
How to Recognize It Rewrite the statement in an unambiguous form and ask whether the argument still follows.

title: Anecdotal Fallacy
description: Using a personal experience or isolated anecdote as sufficient evidence for a broader conclusion.

title: Appeal to Authority
description: Treating an authority's claim as sufficient evidence that the claim must be true.
content:
Visualize │ ▼ "X IS TRUE" │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ THEREFORE │ │ X IS TRUE │ └─────────────┘ ✕ EVIDENCE MISSING Definition An appeal to authority occurs when someone’s status, reputation, or authority is treated as sufficient evidence that a claim is true.
Example “A famous actor says this supplement works, so it must be effective.”
The actor’s fame does not establish expertise in medicine or nutrition.
Why It’s Fallacious Expert testimony can be useful evidence, but an authority’s opinion is not automatically proof. The relevance of the authority’s expertise, the quality of the evidence, and whether there is legitimate expert consensus all matter.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“Is this person’s authority actually relevant to the claim?”
A claim should not be accepted solely because an impressive or famous person made it.

title: Appeal to Emotion
description: Using an emotional response as a substitute for evidence supporting a conclusion.
content:
Definition An appeal to emotion attempts to persuade by provoking feelings rather than providing relevant evidence for the conclusion.
Example “If you really cared about your family, you would support this proposal.”
The statement attempts to connect the proposal to feelings about family rather than demonstrating why the proposal is good.
Why It’s Fallacious Emotions can be relevant to decision-making, but feeling strongly about something does not by itself establish that a particular conclusion is true or that a particular action is justified.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“What evidence supports the conclusion apart from the emotional reaction?”
If the emotional response is doing the work that evidence or reasoning should do, an appeal to emotion may be present.

title: Appeal to Expertise
description: Treating an expert's opinion as decisive evidence without considering whether the expertise, evidence, or consensus supports the claim.

title: Appeal to Fear
description: Using fear of a negative consequence to persuade someone to accept a conclusion without adequate evidence.

title: Appeal to Ignorance
description: Claiming that something must be true because it has not been proven false, or false because it has not been proven true.
content:
Definition An appeal to ignorance argues that a claim is true because nobody has proven it false, or false because nobody has proven it true.
Example “Nobody has proven that extraterrestrial life doesn’t exist, so extraterrestrial life must exist.”
The absence of evidence establishing the claim does not establish the claim itself.
Why It’s Fallacious A lack of evidence for a proposition is not automatically evidence for its opposite. Whether the absence of evidence matters depends on what evidence we would reasonably expect to find if the claim were true.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“Does the argument rely solely on the fact that the opposing claim hasn’t been proven?”
If so, the argument may be appealing to ignorance.

title: Appeal to Nature
description: Assuming that something is good, safe, or desirable because it is natural, or bad because it is unnatural.
content:
Definition An appeal to nature assumes that something is good, safe, healthy, or desirable because it is natural, or that something is bad because it is artificial or unnatural.
Example “This substance is natural, so it can’t be harmful.”
Natural substances can be harmful, and artificial substances can be beneficial.
Why It’s Fallacious Whether something is natural does not by itself determine whether it is good, safe, healthy, or desirable.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“What evidence connects being natural with the property being claimed?”
If naturalness is the only support, the argument may be committing an appeal to nature.

title: Appeal to Pity
description: Using sympathy or compassion as a substitute for evidence supporting a conclusion.

title: Appeal to Probability
description: Treating a probable possibility as though it were certain to be true.

title: Appeal to Tradition
description: Claiming that something is correct, valuable, or necessary simply because it has traditionally been done that way.

title: Bandwagon
description: Claiming that a belief or practice is correct because many people accept or follow it.

title: Base Rate Fallacy
description: Ignoring the general frequency of an event or condition when evaluating specific evidence about it.
content:
Definition The base rate fallacy occurs when someone focuses on specific evidence while neglecting the underlying frequency of the event or condition being considered.
Example Suppose a rare disease affects 1 in 10,000 people. A test is highly accurate, but a positive result occurs.
“The test is 99% accurate, so there’s a 99% chance this person has the disease.”
That conclusion may ignore the very low base rate of the disease.
Why It’s Fallacious Specific evidence needs to be interpreted alongside the underlying probability of the condition.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“How common is this condition before considering the specific evidence?”

title: Begging the Question
description: Using a premise that assumes the conclusion the argument is supposed to establish.
content:
Definition Begging the question occurs when an argument assumes the truth of its conclusion within its premises instead of independently establishing it.
Example “This policy is the best policy because it is better than all the other policies.”
The conclusion that the policy is best is simply restated as a premise.
Why It’s Fallacious The argument does not provide independent support for its conclusion. It assumes what it is supposed to prove.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“Would I have to already accept the conclusion for these premises to work?”
If the answer is yes, the argument may be begging the question.

title: Burden of Proof
description: Failing to recognize that the person making a claim is generally responsible for providing evidence supporting it.

title: Cherry Picking
description: Selecting evidence that supports a conclusion while ignoring relevant evidence that contradicts it.

title: Circular Reasoning
description: Using a conclusion as support for itself, directly or through a chain of reasoning.
content:
Visualize ┌─────────────┐ │ ASSUME A │ └──────┬──────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ THEREFORE │ │ A │ └──────┬──────┘ │ └───────────────┐ │ ▼ ASSUME A Definition Circular reasoning occurs when an argument’s conclusion is used, directly or indirectly, to support one of its own premises.
Example “The newspaper is trustworthy because it says it publishes reliable information, and we know its claim is reliable because the newspaper is trustworthy.”
The argument ultimately relies on itself for support.
Why It’s Fallacious The reasoning never establishes an independent basis for the conclusion.
How to Recognize It Trace the argument backward and ask:
“Does the reasoning eventually depend on the conclusion itself?”
If it does, the argument is circular.

title: Composition
description: Assuming that what is true of individual parts must also be true of the whole.

title: Correlation Does Not Imply Causation
description: Assuming that because two things are correlated, one must have caused the other.
content:
Definition The correlation-causation fallacy occurs when a statistical or observed relationship between two variables is treated as proof that one causes the other.
Example “Ice cream sales increase when drownings increase, so eating ice cream causes drowning.”
Both may increase because hot weather increases both swimming and ice cream consumption.
Why It’s Fallacious Correlation can result from coincidence, a common cause, reverse causation, or other relationships.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“What evidence establishes the causal mechanism?”
A relationship between two variables alone does not establish causation.

title: Division
description: Assuming that what is true of a whole must also be true of each individual part.
content:
Definition The fallacy of division occurs when someone assumes that a property of a group or whole must necessarily apply to every individual member or component of that whole.
Example “The company is extremely wealthy, so every employee who works there must be wealthy.”
The company’s financial resources do not necessarily determine the financial situation of each individual employee.
Why It’s Fallacious Properties of a whole do not necessarily transfer to each of its parts. A group can have a characteristic that none of its individual members possess, or an individual member can differ substantially from the group as a whole.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“Does this property necessarily apply to every individual part of the whole?”
If not, the conclusion may be committing the fallacy of division.

title: Domino Effect
description: Claiming that one event will trigger a chain of events without sufficient evidence that the chain will occur.

title: Equivocation
description: Using the same word or phrase with different meanings within the same argument.

title: False Cause
description: Incorrectly identifying the cause of an event or outcome.

title: False Dilemma
description: Presenting only two options when more possibilities exist.

title: Gambler's Fallacy
description: Believing that an independent random event is more or less likely because previous independent events had different outcomes.
content:
Definition The gambler’s fallacy is the mistaken belief that previous independent random events change the probability of a future independent event.
Example “The coin has landed heads five times in a row, so tails is due next.”
If the coin is fair and the flips are independent, the previous results do not make tails more likely on the next flip.
Why It’s Fallacious Independent random events do not remember previous outcomes.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“Do previous outcomes actually affect the probability of the next outcome?”
If the events are independent, previous results do not change their underlying probabilities.

title: Genetic Fallacy
description: Judging a claim solely by its origin rather than evaluating the claim itself.

title: Hasty Generalization
description: Drawing a broad conclusion from an insufficient or unrepresentative sample.
content:
Visualize SAMPLE ┌───┬───┐ │ A │ A │ └───┴───┘ │ ▼ "ALL A ARE LIKE THIS" │ ✕ SAMPLE TOO SMALL Definition A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from too few observations or from observations that are not representative of the population being discussed.
Example “I visited two restaurants in that city and both were terrible. The restaurants there must all be terrible.”
Two experiences are not enough to establish a conclusion about every restaurant in the city.
Why It’s Fallacious The evidence may be genuine, but the sample is insufficient to support the scope of the conclusion.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“How large and representative is the sample?”
The broader the conclusion, the stronger and more representative the supporting evidence needs to be.

title: Hot-Hand Fallacy
description: Believing that a person is more likely to succeed again after a series of successful outcomes, even when the events are independent.

title: Loaded Question
description: Asking a question that contains an unproven or questionable assumption.

title: Moving the Goalposts
description: Changing the standard of evidence required after the original standard has been met.

title: No True Scotsman
description: Redefining a category to exclude counterexamples to a generalization.

title: Poisoning the Well
description: Discrediting a person or source in advance so that their future arguments will be dismissed regardless of their evidence.
content:
Definition Poisoning the well occurs when someone attempts to discredit a person, source, or group before their argument is presented, encouraging others to reject what they say regardless of the evidence.
Example “Don’t listen to anything Alex says about the project. He’s always been a terrible employee.”
Alex’s past behavior does not establish that everything Alex says about the project is false.
Why It’s Fallacious Discrediting a person in advance does not establish that their future claims are false. Each claim should be evaluated based on its evidence and reasoning.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“Is this information being presented to evaluate the argument, or to make me reject the speaker before hearing the argument?”
If the goal is to discredit the source before considering the evidence, poisoning the well may be involved.

title: Post Hoc
description: Assuming that because one event happened after another, the first event caused the second.
content:
Definition Post hoc reasoning assumes that because one event occurred after another, the earlier event caused the later event.
Example “I wore my lucky shirt and then our team won. The shirt caused us to win.”
The sequence of events does not establish a causal relationship.
Why It’s Fallacious Events can occur in sequence for many reasons. Establishing causation requires more than simply showing that one event happened before another.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“What evidence shows that the first event caused the second?”
If the only evidence is that one event happened first, the argument is likely committing a post hoc fallacy.

title: Red Herring
description: Introducing an irrelevant issue to distract from the argument being discussed.
content:
Visualize ORIGINAL QUESTION │ ▼ ┌──────────────┐ │ ? │ └──────────────┘ │ │ └──────────────► 🐟 │ ▼ UNRELATED TOPIC │ ▼ DISTRACTION Definition A red herring is an irrelevant point introduced into an argument to distract from the original issue.
Example “Why are you concerned about the company’s environmental record? They’re one of the largest employers in the region.”
The company’s employment numbers do not answer the question about its environmental record.
Why It’s Fallacious The new issue may be interesting or even true, but it does not address the question under discussion.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“Does this response actually address the original question or claim?”
If the discussion has shifted to an unrelated subject without resolving the original issue, a red herring may be involved.

title: Shifting the Burden of Proof
description: Demanding that others disprove a claim instead of providing evidence for the claim being made.

title: Slippery Slope
description: Claiming that one event will inevitably lead to extreme consequences without sufficient evidence.
content:
Visualize SMALL ACTION │ ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ STEP 1 │ └─────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ STEP 2 │ └─────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ STEP 3 │ └─────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ ABSURD END │ │ RESULT │ └─────────────┘ ✕ MISSING LINKS Definition A slippery slope argument claims that allowing or causing one event will inevitably lead to a chain of increasingly serious consequences without adequately establishing that the chain will occur.
Example “If we allow students to use phones during lunch, eventually they’ll use them during every class and nobody will pay attention anymore.”
The argument assumes a chain of events without establishing that each step will necessarily follow.
Why It’s Fallacious Consequences can follow from one another, but the argument must establish why the proposed chain is sufficiently likely.
How to Recognize It Look for a sequence such as:
A → B → C → D → extreme outcome
Then ask whether there is evidence supporting each important step in the chain.

title: Special Pleading
description: Applying a standard inconsistently by making an unsupported exception for a favored case.

title: Stereotyping
description: Applying a generalized belief about a group to an individual without sufficient evidence.

title: Straw Man
description: Misrepresenting someone's argument so that it is easier to attack.
content:
Visualize ACTUAL ARGUMENT │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ "A" │ └─────────────┘ │ │ DISTORT ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ "B" │ ← ATTACK └─────────────┘ ✕ ACTUAL ARGUMENT UNANSWERED Definition A straw man fallacy occurs when someone misrepresents another person’s argument, position, or claim and then attacks the distorted version instead of addressing the original argument.
Example “You think we should reduce unnecessary military spending? So you want to leave the country completely defenseless.”
The original argument was about reducing unnecessary spending, not eliminating the military.
Why It’s Fallacious The response attacks a position that the other person did not actually make. Even if the distorted version is easily defeated, that does not establish that the original argument is wrong.
How to Recognize It Compare the response with the original claim. Ask:
“Did they actually argue that?”
If the response relies on an exaggerated, simplified, or distorted version of the original position, it may be a straw man.

title: Texas Sharpshooter
description: Selecting patterns or evidence after the fact and treating the selected pattern as if it had been predicted in advance.
content:
Definition The Texas Sharpshooter fallacy occurs when someone searches through data for a pattern, selects a pattern that appears interesting, and then presents it as meaningful without accounting for the other patterns that could have been selected.
Example A person records dozens of unrelated measurements, finds a subset that happens to form a striking pattern, and then claims the pattern proves a meaningful connection.
Why It’s Fallacious Large or complex datasets can contain apparent patterns purely by chance. Selecting the interesting pattern after examining the data can make random coincidence appear significant.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“Was this pattern predicted before the data were examined?”
Also ask what other patterns were possible but ignored.

title: Tu Quoque
description: Rejecting criticism by accusing the critic of the same behavior.
content:
Visualize CLAIM │ ▼ "YOU SHOULD NOT DO X" │ ▼ "YOU DO X!" │ ✕ ORIGINAL CLAIM UNANSWERED Definition Tu quoque is a form of ad hominem reasoning that responds to criticism by pointing out that the person making the criticism has behaved inconsistently with their own claim.
Example “You say I shouldn’t smoke, but you smoke too.”
The critic’s behavior does not determine whether smoking is harmful.
Why It’s Fallacious A person can make a correct argument even if they fail to follow their own advice. Hypocrisy may be worth discussing, but it does not refute the underlying claim.
How to Recognize It Ask:
“Does the critic’s behavior actually disprove their argument?”
If not, pointing out their inconsistency does not address the substance of the claim.

title: Whataboutism
description: Responding to criticism by pointing to another person's wrongdoing instead of addressing the original criticism.
